learn.hook: Every morning, lakhs of people pour into Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru by train, bus and metro. Why do so many people move to cities?
points: Urbanisation is the increase in the share of a country's people who live in towns and cities.
Cities grow because people migrate from villages for jobs, education and health care, because of natural growth of the city population, and because villages near cities become part of them.
In India, statutory towns are places with a municipal corporation, municipality, cantonment board or notified town area.
A census town is a place with at least 5,000 people, a density of at least 400 people per sq km, and at least 75% of male main workers doing non-farm work.

Towns and cities are run by urban local bodies: municipal corporations for big cities (headed by a mayor), municipalities for smaller towns, and nagar panchayats for areas changing from rural to urban.

example.q: Think it through: A place has 8,000 people, a density of 500 per sq km, and 80% of its male main workers do non-farm work. It has no municipality. Is it a census town?
steps: Population: 8,000 is at least 5,000. ✔
Density: 500 is at least 400 per sq km. ✔
Non-farm male main workers: 80% is at least 75%. ✔
All three conditions are met.
example.answer: Yes, it is a census town.

learn.reallife: When a new metro line or IT park opens near a village, the village often grows into a busy town within a few years.

steps: A census town needs at least 5,000 people.

quiz.q: What minimum density (people per sq km) is required for a census town?
quiz.explain: The density must be at least 400 per sq km.

options: Jobs and better services like schools and hospitals
quiz.explain: Cities offer more work in industries and services.

Answer: 75%

teach.ask: Gappu wonders what makes a place a 'town'. Explain urbanisation and towns to Gappu.
teach.praise: So towns need enough people, density and non-farm jobs! And mayors look after cities.
teach.nudge: Why do cities grow? What makes a place a town, and who runs it?

revise.summary: Urbanisation is the rising share of people living in towns and cities, through migration, natural growth and absorbing nearby villages. Statutory towns have a municipal body; census towns meet population, density and non-farm work conditions. Cities are run by urban local bodies.
focus: Urban local bodies and who heads them
remember: Census town: at least 5,000 people, density at least 400 per sq km, at least 75% male main workers in non-farm work
Statutory town: has municipal corporation, municipality, cantonment board or notified town area
traps: A place with a municipality is a statutory, not census, town
The density rule is 400, not 4,000, per sq km
The mayor, not the sarpanch, heads a municipal corporation

topics.title: Kinds of cities: old, planned and new

learn.hook: Over 4,000 years ago, Harappan cities had straight streets and covered drains. Some modern Indian cities are still planned the same careful way!
points: Cities of the Harappan Civilisation, such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Lothal, had planned streets in a grid and good drainage.
Many towns grew around a special function: temple towns like Madurai and Puri, port towns like Surat and Kozhikode, and capital cities like Delhi and Fatehpur Sikri.
Jaipur was planned in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, with wide streets in a grid. Its walled city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
During colonial rule, Bombay (Mumbai), Madras (Chennai) and Calcutta (Kolkata) grew as port cities and trade centres.

After independence, new planned cities were built, such as Chandigarh, designed by the architect Le Corbusier. Some cities are known for one main activity, like Jamshedpur for steel and Bengaluru for information technology.

example.q: Think it through: Why did port towns like Surat and Kozhikode grow into big trading centres?
steps: They were on the coast with harbours for ships.
Ships brought goods from other countries and carried Indian goods away.
Traders, workers, sailors and craftspeople came to live there.
Markets, warehouses and services grew, and so did the town.
example.answer: Their harbours made them centres of sea trade, which drew traders and workers and made the towns grow.

learn.reallife: Chandigarh is divided into numbered sectors, each planned with its own market, school and park, so people can find addresses easily.

quiz.explain: Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur as a planned city.
steps: Sawai Jai Singh II planned Jaipur in 1727.

quiz.q: Madurai and Puri are examples of:
quiz.explain: They grew around famous temples.
steps: Madurai and Puri grew around famous temples.
So they are temple towns.
Answer: Temple towns

quiz.q: Jamshedpur is best known for:
quiz.explain: Jamshedpur grew around a large steel plant.

Answer: Steel

quiz.explain: Their ports linked India's trade with the world.
steps: Under colonial rule, Bombay, Madras and Calcutta grew as port cities and trade centres.
Answer: Port cities and trade centres

quiz.q: Which of these is a Harappan city in Gujarat?

options: Many information technology companies are based there
quiz.explain: Thousands of IT firms and startups work from Bengaluru.

Answer: Many information technology companies are based there
quiz.mistake: Does not link cities with their main activity

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why cities look so different. Explain old, planned and new cities to Gappu.
teach.praise: From Harappa to Chandigarh: cities have stories! Gappu loves the grid streets.
teach.nudge: What were Harappan cities like? Can you name a temple town, a port town and a planned city?

revise.summary: India's cities include planned Harappan cities, towns grown around a function (temple, port, capital), planned Jaipur (1727), colonial port cities and new planned cities like Chandigarh (Le Corbusier). Some cities are known for one activity, like Jamshedpur (steel) and Bengaluru (IT).
remember: Harappan cities: grid streets, drainage (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Lothal)
traps: Le Corbusier designed Chandigarh, not Jaipur
Madurai is a temple town, not a port city
Dholavira is in Gujarat, not Punjab

learn.hook: Traffic jams, garbage heaps and water tankers: cities give us jobs and comforts, but they also face big problems. Can we fix them?
points: When cities grow faster than housing, many people live in slums with crowded homes and poor water and sanitation.
More vehicles cause traffic jams and air pollution. Public transport like buses and metro rail can carry many people using less road space. India's first metro opened in Kolkata in 1984.
Cities produce huge amounts of waste. Separating wet and dry waste at home, composting and recycling reduce the load on landfills.
Concrete and roads cover the soil, so rainwater cannot soak in. This causes urban flooding and falling groundwater. Rainwater harvesting, lakes and green spaces help.
Cities are often hotter than nearby villages because concrete and asphalt soak up heat. This is called the urban heat island effect. Trees and parks help to cool them.

example.q: Think it through: Why does a city get flooded after heavy rain even if it is not near a river?
steps: Roads, buildings and pavements cover most of the ground.
Rainwater cannot soak into the soil.
Drains get blocked by plastic and waste, or are too small.
So water collects on the roads.
example.answer: Hard surfaces stop rain from soaking in, and blocked or small drains cannot carry it away, so water floods the streets.

learn.reallife: Many housing societies now have separate green and blue bins for wet and dry waste, and metro trains in cities like Delhi, Chennai and Kochi carry lakhs of riders daily.

games.title: Match the problem to a solution

quiz.q: Why do slums often grow in cities?
options: Cities grow faster than affordable housing
quiz.explain: Migrants who cannot afford homes settle in crowded areas.
steps: Cities grow faster than affordable housing.
Migrants who cannot afford homes settle in crowded slums.
Answer: Cities grow faster than affordable housing
quiz.mistake: Does not link slums with housing shortage

quiz.q: Which city had India's first metro rail, opened in 1984?
quiz.explain: The Kolkata Metro began in 1984; Delhi's opened in 2002.
steps: India's first metro rail opened in Kolkata in 1984.
Delhi's opened in 2002.
Answer: Kolkata
quiz.mistake: Assumes the capital had the first metro

quiz.q: Why does public transport reduce traffic and pollution?
options: It increases the number of cars
One bus or metro train carries many people using less road space
quiz.explain: Fewer private vehicles mean less congestion and fewer exhaust fumes.
steps: One bus or metro train carries many people using less road space.
Fewer private vehicles means less traffic and pollution.
Answer: One bus or metro train carries many people using less road space
quiz.mistake: Does not see the benefit of shared transport

quiz.q: What is the urban heat island effect?
options: Cities being hotter than nearby rural areas
quiz.explain: Concrete and asphalt absorb heat and release it slowly.
steps: The urban heat island effect: cities are hotter than nearby rural areas.
Concrete and asphalt soak up heat.
Answer: Cities being hotter than nearby rural areas
quiz.mistake: Takes the term literally

quiz.q: Which is wet waste?
quiz.explain: Wet waste is kitchen and food waste that can be composted.
steps: Wet waste is kitchen and food waste that can be composted.
Vegetable peels are wet waste.
Answer: Vegetable peels
quiz.mistake: Mixes up wet and dry waste

quiz.q: Why do many cities face urban flooding?
options: Hard surfaces stop rainwater from soaking in and drains get blocked
quiz.explain: Concrete surfaces and blocked drains leave water on roads.
steps: Concrete and roads stop rainwater soaking in, and drains get blocked.
So water floods city streets.
Answer: Hard surfaces stop rainwater from soaking in and drains get blocked
quiz.mistake: Thinks flooding happens only near rivers

quiz.q: Which action helps to recharge groundwater in cities?
quiz.explain: Rainwater harvesting stores rain and lets it soak into the ground.
steps: Rainwater harvesting stores rain and lets it soak into the ground.
So it recharges groundwater.
Answer: Rainwater harvesting
quiz.mistake: Does not know how groundwater is recharged

quiz.q: Which is the best way a family can reduce the garbage sent to landfills?
options: Burn all waste on the street
Separate wet and dry waste and compost the wet waste
Mix all waste in one bag
quiz.explain: Segregation lets wet waste be composted and dry waste be recycled.
steps: Separating wet and dry waste lets wet waste be composted and dry waste recycled.
This sends less garbage to landfills.
Answer: Separate wet and dry waste and compost the wet waste
quiz.mistake: Thinks burning or dumping solves waste problems

teach.ask: Gappu visited a big city and got stuck in traffic and smoke. Explain city problems and how we can solve them.
teach.praise: Metro rides, compost bins and more trees: Gappu has a plan for a happier city!
teach.nudge: What problems do cities face? What can people and governments do about them?

revise.summary: Fast-growing cities face slums, traffic and pollution, waste, urban flooding and the urban heat island effect. Solutions include public transport (India's first metro: Kolkata, 1984), waste segregation and composting, rainwater harvesting, lakes and trees.
remember: Urban heat island: cities hotter than nearby villages
Segregate wet and dry waste; compost wet waste
traps: Delhi did not have India's first metro; Kolkata did
Burning waste is not a solution
Paving open spaces makes flooding worse
